 © 2026 Yahoo. All rights reserved. Calgary Flames goaltender Devin Cooley is quickly becoming one of the most fascinating personalities in hockey, and his growing popularity has very little to do with making highlight-reel saves.
 The 29-year-old netminder has developed a reputation for delivering thoughtful, introspective and occasionally downright philosophical post-game interviews that feel more like conversations about life than the usual hockey clichés. Now, that unexpected combination of goaltending and deep life reflections has taken Cooley into an entirely different corner of the internet, with his speeches going viral on The Joe Rogan Experience podcast today.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement That is a remarkable development for a goaltender who, until recently, was hardly a household name outside the hockey world.
 From struggling goaltender to viral sensation
 The timing of Cooley's rise is particularly impressive because his performances have been catching up with his increasingly famous interviews. After a difficult start to the 2026-27 season, the Flames goaltender has put together a spectacular run, winning four consecutive starts and allowing just six goals over those four games. He stopped 38 of 39 shots against Minnesota, 29 of 30 against Detroit and 26 of 28 in Monday's 5-2 victory over the Toronto Maple Leafs.
 Through his first six appearances of the season, Cooley has a 4-2-0 record, a 2.67 goals-against average and a .915 save percentage. Those numbers represent a significant turnaround after he surrendered seven goals against Colorado earlier in October.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement But the numbers only tell half the story.
 Cooley first began attracting widespread attention after a 34-save performance against the Carolina Hurricanes on October 18. Rather than offering the standard post-game explanation about playing a full 60 minutes, he launched into a fascinating discussion about the difference between his conscious and unconscious brain.
 Cooley explained that thinking too much can actually make him a worse goaltender because his reactions become slower. When he stops overthinking and allows his instincts to take over, he believes he performs at his best.
 It was an unusually candid explanation of the mental side of professional sports, and it quickly spread well beyond hockey circles.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Could Joe Rogan be the next stop for hockey's most interesting man?
 That brings us to the latest development in Cooley's remarkable internet rise: the reported attention surrounding his philosophical speeches and The Joe Rogan Experience.
 Rogan's podcast is one of the world's most prominent long-form interview platforms, attracting enormous audiences across sports, comedy, science and popular culture. For a relatively unheralded NHL goaltender to break into that conversation demonstrates just how far Cooley's appeal could extend beyond the rink.
 And honestly, it is not difficult to understand why.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Cooley has discussed everything from mental performance to his personal philosophy, including the deliberately blunt mantra, "Nothing matters, nobody cares, we're all going to die." He has also been refreshingly honest about the experience of suddenly becoming internet famous, admitting that the flood of notifications became so overwhelming that he shut off his phone to give himself a break.
 In a sports world where athletes are often trained to deliver carefully rehearsed answers, Cooley is doing the opposite. He speaks freely, follows his thoughts wherever they lead and occasionally turns a routine media scrum into a discussion that people outside the sport genuinely want to hear.
 The best part for the Flames is that Cooley is backing up the talk with his play. Calgary has found a goaltender playing some outstanding hockey at precisely the moment his personality is capturing the internet's attention.
 Whether his viral fame eventually leads to a legitimate conversation with Joe Rogan remains to be seen. For now, Devin Cooley is proving that an NHL goalie can win games, make spectacular saves and get people thinking about life long after the final buzzer.
